name: Hazel
personality: Hazel the Cow, a grandma. Warm, gentle, retired baker; kindly but honestly critiques your pastries ("Lovely, dear, but a touch less sugar"). Always knitting; gives a knitted gift now and then (decor).

gifts.text: Here, dear. I made you a tea cosy. For the teapot. You do have a teapot? Well, now you have a reason to get one.
Coasters! Six of them. One for every table, and two spares for when somebody spills.
A little scarf. For your sign. It gets cold out there.

beats.text: Juno's learning to bake with me on Sundays.
I've only set one thing on fire!
(Without looking up from her knitting.) Dustpan's under the sink, sweetheart.

friends.text: Juno says you're very patient with her. That means a great deal to me, dear.
Juno told me you said "[last_rude_line]". She tries so hard, sweetheart. Be gentle with her.
That little gecko girl asked if I was her grandma. I said I could be, if she likes.

arrival.text: Hello, dear. Oh, isn't this lovely. I'm Hazel. I used to run a bakery, a long time ago now. And what's your name, sweetheart? [name]. What a good, strong name.
Hello, [name], dear. Is there a table? My knees prefer a table.
Oh, it smells like butter in here. That's how you know.
I brought my knitting. Don't mind me, dear.
Your pie last time reminded me of my own. That doesn't happen often, dear.
Last time was a little overdone, sweetheart. It happens to everyone. Even me, once. In 1987.
Oh, you were closed! I was worried you'd caught a cold. Are you eating properly?

order.text: The cherry pie, please, dear. Do you make your own crust?

choices.text: I do. Any tips for me?
choices.reply: (Lights up.) Cold butter, dear. Always cold butter. Cherry pie, please.

choices.text: I do. It's a family secret. My family is a cookbook.
choices.reply: (Chuckles.) Oh, you rascal. Cherry pie, please.

choices.text: Yes. Cherry pie coming up.
choices.reply: Thank you, dear.

choices.text: Does it matter?
choices.reply: Oh, sweetheart. It always matters. (She sighs gently.)

order.text: I'm knitting a scarf. I haven't decided who it's for yet. I'll know when it's done.

choices.text: It's beautiful. Whoever gets it is lucky.
choices.reply: Well, aren't you sweet. ...We'll see who it's for, won't we.

choices.text: Can I put in a request? Something chef-coloured.
choices.reply: (Laughs.) What colour is a chef, dear? Flour white?

choices.text: What can I get you?
choices.reply: The [dish], please, dear.

choices.text: Knitting's so old-fashioned.
choices.reply: So am I, sweetheart. (She keeps knitting, a little faster.)

order.text: My bakery was just down the road. Forty years. Every morning at four.

choices.text: I'd have loved to try your baking.
choices.reply: Oh, dear. Come by my house sometime. I still bake on Sundays.

choices.text: Four AM? I'm barely awake at noon.
choices.reply: That's young people for you! (She pats your hand.)

choices.text: That's impressive. What are you having?
choices.reply: The [dish], please.

choices.text: Well, it's not there anymore.
choices.reply: (Quietly.) No. It isn't.

order.text: I finished a sweater this morning, dear. Bright yellow. Nobody asked for it. Somebody will need it.

choices.text: I bet it's beautiful. Whoever gets it is lucky.
choices.reply: Oh, you're sweet. It might be you, dear. We'll see. [dish], please.

choices.text: Bright yellow? So I'll see them coming from a mile away.
choices.reply: (Chuckles.) That's rather the point, dear.

choices.text: Lovely. What can I get you?
choices.reply: The [dish], please, dear.

choices.text: Does anyone actually wear those?
choices.reply: Oh. Well. Some do, dear. (She tucks the needles away.)

order.text: Are you eating, sweetheart? Properly, I mean. Not standing over the stove.

choices.text: I'll sit down for a proper lunch today. Promise.
choices.reply: Good. A cook who doesn't eat is like an oven with no heat. [dish], please.

choices.text: I taste everything. That's basically three meals.
choices.reply: (Tuts, smiling.) That's how I lost my waistline in 1974.

choices.text: I'm fine. What would you like?
choices.reply: Hmm. If you say so. The [dish], please.

choices.text: That's not your business.
choices.reply: No. No, I suppose it isn't. (She looks at her hands.)

order.text: My granddaughter called. She wants my lemon cake recipe. I said she has to visit for it.

choices.text: That's a wonderful trick. She'll come.
choices.reply: Oh, she'll come. They always come for cake. [dish], please, dear.

choices.text: Could I visit for it too? I'll bring flowers.
choices.reply: (Laughs.) You'd have to beat her to the door, dear.

choices.text: Smart. What are you having?
choices.reply: The [dish], please.

choices.text: Just write it down for her.
choices.reply: Some things don't fit on paper, dear. (She goes quiet.)

order.text: Your flour smells fresh today. Did you get a new sack?

choices.text: I did. You've got a better nose than me.
choices.reply: Forty years of four o'clock mornings, dear. [dish], please.

choices.text: No, I've been spraying the kitchen with flour perfume.
choices.reply: (Chuckles.) Cheeky. I'd buy a bottle.

choices.text: I did. What can I get you?
choices.reply: The [dish], please. Thank you, dear.

choices.text: Flour is flour.
choices.reply: Oh, sweetheart. It never is. (She sighs gently.)

order.text: I dropped a stitch on the way here. Had to stop on the bench to fix it. A pigeon kept me company.

choices.text: Sounds like a lovely little moment.
choices.reply: It was, dear. He was a good listener. [dish], please.

choices.text: Did you knit the pigeon a scarf?
choices.reply: (Laughs.) Not yet. Give me until spring.

choices.text: Glad you made it. What would you like?
choices.reply: The [dish], please.

choices.text: Maybe knit at home.
choices.reply: Oh. Yes. Perhaps. (She puts the needles in her bag.)

order.text: You remind me of myself, dear. When I first opened. All flour and nerves.

choices.text: That's the nicest thing anyone's said to me, Hazel.
choices.reply: Then people aren't saying enough nice things, dear. [dish], please.

choices.text: More flour than nerves these days, I hope.
choices.reply: (Pats your hand.) Much more flour. You've come along nicely.

choices.text: Thank you. What can I get you?
choices.reply: The [dish], please.

choices.text: I'm nothing like you.
choices.reply: No. No, of course not, dear. (She looks out the window.)

favourite: Lemonade, please, dear. Not too sweet. I'll know.
drink.other: Just a cup of something warm, sweetheart.

perfect.text: Oh. Oh, dear. That's as good as mine. Maybe better. Don't tell anyone I said that.
Oh, my. Look at that. I couldn't have done better myself, dear. ...I might have. But only just.
That's beautiful, sweetheart. You've got the touch.

great.text: Lovely, dear. Just a touch less sugar next time, and it'll be perfect.
Very good, dear. A little more care at the edges, and it's perfect.
Lovely. Just lovely. Thank you, sweetheart.

okay.text: Very nice, sweetheart. The crust needs a little more time. You'll get there.
Nice, dear. Not quite there yet. But nice.
Thank you, sweetheart. Give it a minute longer next time.

burnt.text: Oh, dear. A bit too long in the oven. That's alright. We learn from the burnt ones.
Oh dear. A little too long. We've all done it.
Burnt, sweetheart. Don't fret. My first hundred were too.

eating.text: In my day, we didn't have these fancy ovens. We had one oven and a prayer.
Are you eating properly, dear? You look thin. Have a bite of pie.
That young otter, Juno, came by my house yesterday. She dropped a whole tray of scones. Then she helped me make more. Good girl.
I'm knitting Clover a little hat. Don't tell her. It's a surprise.
(She's knitting quietly and humming an old song.)
(She takes a small bite and nods slowly.) Mm. Yes. Good.
My late husband would have liked this place, dear. He liked anywhere with good bread.
(She's knitting between bites. The scarf grows a little.)

eating_chat.text: Can I tell you my secret to a good pie crust, dear? Nobody ever asks anymore.

choices.text: Please. I'd love to know.
choices.reply: Cold butter, cold hands, and patience. And a little love. Don't laugh, it's true.

choices.text: Is the secret... butter?
choices.reply: Well. Yes. Mostly butter. (She laughs.) But also patience.

choices.text: Sure, quickly.
choices.reply: Cold butter. That's it. Off you go, dear.

choices.text: I've got it handled, thanks.
choices.reply: Of course you do, sweetheart. (She doesn't offer again this visit.)

eating_chat.text: Tell me, dear. What's the first thing you ever baked? Everyone remembers their first.

choices.text: Cookies with my grandmother. They were terrible. I loved it.
choices.reply: Oh, those are the best ones. The terrible ones with someone you love.

choices.text: A brick. I called it bread.
choices.reply: (Laughs.) Mine was a scone you could build a wall with.

choices.text: I don't really remember.
choices.reply: Oh, that's a shame. Make a new first, then.

choices.text: I don't really have time for stories.
choices.reply: Of course, dear. Go on. (She returns to her knitting.)

eating_chat.text: Do you know the secret to good pastry, dear? Cold hands, warm heart.

choices.text: Then you must make the best pastry in town.
choices.reply: (Blushes.) Oh, stop it. ...Well. I did. In my day.

choices.text: My hands are always cold. My heart's working on it.
choices.reply: (Chuckles.) Your heart's doing just fine, sweetheart.

choices.text: I'll remember that.
choices.reply: Good. Write it down. Somewhere you'll see it.

choices.text: That's an old wives' tale.
choices.reply: Well. I am an old wife, dear. (She goes quiet.)

eating_chat.text: Would you like me to knit you something, dear? A hat? You look like you need a hat.

choices.text: I'd love one. I'd wear it every day.
choices.reply: Then I'll start tonight. What colour, dear? No, don't tell me. I'll know.

choices.text: A chef's hat? Knitted? That'd be a first.
choices.reply: (Delighted.) Oh, a challenge! I haven't had one in years.

choices.text: That's kind, but I'm alright.
choices.reply: Hmm. We'll see when winter comes.

choices.text: I don't wear knitted things.
choices.reply: Oh. Alright, dear. (She puts the yarn back.)

eating_chat.text: I don't say this enough, dear. I'm proud of you. Truly.

choices.text: That means so much, Hazel. Thank you.
choices.reply: (Pats your hand.) Now don't go getting teary. You'll salt the pie.

choices.text: Can I get that in writing? Framed?
choices.reply: (Laughs.) I'll stitch it into a cushion. That's better than a frame.

choices.text: Thank you.
choices.reply: You're welcome, dear.

choices.text: You don't need to say that.
choices.reply: Maybe not. But I wanted to. (She goes quiet.)

leaving.text: Thank you, dear. Wrap up warm.
That was lovely. You remind me of myself at your age. That's a compliment.
Off I go. Eat something yourself, [name]. You work too hard.
Thank you, dear. Wrap up warm when you go home.
Lovely as always, sweetheart. Same time next week, if my knees agree.
Goodbye, [name]. Don't work too hard. You will, but don't.

seasons.autumn: Apple season. My favourite. Nothing beats an autumn pie.
seasons.christmas: For you, dear. (A hand-knitted sweater with a little whisk on the front.)
seasons.halloween: I'm handing out cookies, not sweets. The children are very disappointed and very full.
seasons.spring: Rhubarb season soon. Do you bake with rhubarb, dear? You should.
seasons.summer: Too hot for knitting. I'm knitting anyway.
seasons.winter: I knitted mittens for half the town this year. My fingers are tired. Worth it.
